newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arabs looking at restrictions on talks with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Arabs looking at restrictions on talks with Israel.

text.p: Arab states are looking at proposals to limit negotiations with Israel and Syria has revived its longstanding proposal that other states join its boycott of multilateral talks, diplomats said on Saturday.
The ideas came to the fore during the past 24 hours of meetings in Cairo by Arab foreign ministers, they said.

The sources said ministers from the Arab parties to the peace talks, plus two Gulf states and two North African states would discuss several urgent proposals on how to respond to what Arabs see as intransigence by the new Israeli government.
"The proposals are on cutting the negotiations down to size and adopting the same method in the negotiations as Israel is doing now," one source said.
Arab states say Israel is trying to back out of agreements made by the previous leftwing government of prime ministers Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin.

The sources said the group of ministers would present finished proposals at a final session of the Arab League ministerial meetings on Sunday and the proposals would then go to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in his capacity as chairman of the Arab summit held in Cairo in June.

Some of the ministerial meetings are to assess how Israel has responded to the summit's message that Arab states might reconsider steps towards normal relations with Israel if the new government does not fulfil old agreements.

The sources said that at a meeting on Saturday evening, in effect their fifth in two days, the ministers would look at the Syrian proposal to freeze multilateral talks with Israel in retaliation for the new government's policies.
If the other ministers agreed, this would spell the end of Egypt's plan to hold an economic summit in Cairo in November.
Egypt has already said that holding the conference on time depends on progress towards Middle East peace but it also says it very much wants the event to go ahead.

Syria and its ally Lebanon never took part in the multilateral tracks of the peace talks launched in Madrid in 1991, arguing it made no sense to include Israel in regional cooperation until it signed full peace agreements.
But Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, asked again on Saturday what the prospects were for the Middle East economic conference, told reporters the ministers had not discussed it.
At a special session on Palestinian affairs, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Saturday complained Israel was only play-acting at peace.

"There is an impasse not only on the Palestinian track but the Syrian and Lebanese tracks, where nothing has been implemented concerning the agreements signed and agreed upon," Arafat told reporters at the end of the meeting.

In the first formal resolution from the meeting, the ministers condemned Turkish, Iranian or any other intervention in northern Iraq and said a proposed Turkish buffer zone there would be a violation of Iraqi territory.

An Arab League statement said the ministers described the situation in northern Iraq as serious as a result of what it called "Turkish violations on the pretext of setting up a so-called security belt or danger zone".

"The Council (of ministers) expressed its extreme concern at developments in the situation as a result of regional interventions which threaten the unity, security and safety of the territory of the Iraqi Republic," it said. "The Council
strongly condemns the intervention by some neighbouring countries in the internal affairs of the territory of an Arab League member state," it added.
The statement mentioned Turkey by name but not Iran, which has supported the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan against the Baghdad-backed Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).
